name: Search page
markup: No html in this file. Each variant below carries the path to its own markup at r/search-page/<variant>.html — fetch the one you need.
description: The whole-page answer to a query typed into the global search: the query echoed as the one h1, the results grouped by record type with a count on every group, the facets that narrow them, and the states the page is in when there is nothing to show yet or nothing to show at all.
when_to_use: Where the global search lands when somebody presses Enter — a whole page at a URL, with the query in it, bookmarkable and sendable to the person who asked. The first line to draw is against command-palette, and it is the line between an accelerator and an answer. The palette is the ⌘K overlay: it opens over the page you are already on, it is a shortcut to a record you know exists, it shows about ten rows because that is what fits above a software keyboard, and it is gone the moment you pick one. Reach for it when the user knows what they want and wants to be there in three keystrokes. Reach for this page when the palette was not enough — when the query matched more than an overlay can hold, when the user wants to narrow by type, plant, status, date or value, or when the answer is a set of records they are going to read rather than one record they are going to jump to. The palette links here rather than truncating silently: its last row is "See all results for …", and this page is what that row opens. The second line is against index-page, and it is the difference between searching and filtering. Typing into the box at the top of the purchase order register is a filter — one record type, the register's own columns, the register's own sort, and the result is still the register. This page searches every register at once and does not know which one the answer is in, which is the whole reason it groups; the moment the user does know, index-page is the better screen and its filter is the better control, which is why every group heading here links to it. The third is combobox, which is searching to fill in a field: the typing is a search, but the outcome is a value posted with a form and nothing about it is a page. A query that could not be answered at all — the index is down, the request timed out — is error-page, not the empty variant here.
rules: A result is a record and not a document. This is not web search and there is no snippet: a purchase order row carries the number, the vendor, the value, the date and the status, because that is what the buyer recognises the order from, and it is the same set of facts the register would have shown them. So the row shape is designed per record type — five row shapes, not one generic row with a title and two grey lines under it. A generic row is cheaper to build and it costs the user the one thing they came for, which is to tell at a glance which of the fourteen orders is theirs.

Grouping beats ranking, and it is the opposite call from the one command-palette makes on the same facts. Type 4821 into a procurement system and the number is an item code, a GRN, part of a PO number and a substring of somebody's GSTIN. The palette ranks those into one list because it has ten rows to spend and no room for headings, and it pays for that by writing the kind onto every row. A page has a screen: fourteen purchase orders, three items and one vendor is a more useful answer than eighteen rows in score order, because the user almost always knows which kind of thing they are after and a heading with a count answers that before they read a single row. The heading is also the control — it is where the narrowing starts.

Groups are ordered by the best match inside them, never by size. An exact hit on one item code outranks 186 orders that merely quote it, and a group of one goes first when its one is the answer. Sorting by count puts the noisiest register on top on every query, and sorting by a score that can tie makes the page reshuffle between two searches that looked the same. The tiebreak is a fixed register order, so equal scores never swap.

Three rows per group, and the count is the rest of the answer. With five kinds on one screen the point of a group is its shape and its size, not its contents; the fourth row costs the group below it its heading, and a page whose fifth heading is under the fold is a page that has hidden a whole register. Where a group is truncated, the header carries the link — "See all 186" — and that link is the route to the scoped page.

One group with 400 results is the normal case and not an edge. An item code is on every order line ever raised for that item, so searching one gives 186 purchase orders and always will. The page does not page inside a group and must not: a pager under one heading with four more groups below it is a control that moves rows nobody is reading. It truncates, states the true count, and hands the whole thing to the scoped page, which has one type, one sort, one pager and room for the register's own columns.

Where the field that matched is not on the row, the row says which field it was. A vendor whose name has nothing to do with the query, sitting in the results because the digits are inside its GSTIN, reads as noise and takes the credibility of the whole page with it; the same row with "matched on GSTIN 24AACCS4821K1ZP" under it is the most useful row on the page. The clause is grey and it is a fact, not a highlight — nothing in this system paints a fill behind matched characters.

The query is the URL and the whole query is in it. /search/?q=MS-4821&type=order&plant=silvassa, always a GET, so Back works, a narrowed result is a link somebody can send to the buyer who asked, and the export of a result set cannot disagree with the screen. Facet state that lives only in the browser is the defect: the page looks right and cannot be shared, and the second person to look at it sees a different answer.

Every result row is a real anchor and the whole row is the target — one stretched after:absolute after:inset-0 link in the identifying cell, with any second link inside the row lifted above it on relative z-10. This is exactly where the page differs from the palette, and it is the reason the palette has to link here: nothing inside role="option" may be focusable, so a palette row is a div and a handler, with no middle-click, no open-in-a-new-tab and no status bar saying where it goes. A search result is something people open in six tabs.

A query that is exactly one document number does not redirect. The temptation is real — one obvious answer, so send them to it — and it costs the two most common reasons anybody types a number into a search box: to find out whether the record exists at all, and to see what else refers to it. Redirecting drops them inside a record they did not choose to open, makes Back part of the workflow, and hides the fourteen receipts and invoices that were the actual question. The palette may navigate on Enter because a person picked a row; the page may not, because nobody picked anything. The exact hit gets its own region at the top instead, and it is not repeated in the group below it — a record drawn twice on one page is a record somebody opens twice.

The empty result is the variant that earns this entry. Nobody complains about a search that works. It says what was searched — five registers, by number, code, name and GSTIN, and not the text of notes, line descriptions or attachments — because "no results" leaves somebody retyping the same string, and it offers the loosened query with its real count rather than running it silently. A search that quietly widens is one whose result count nobody can reproduce, and the user cannot tell whether the seven rows in front of them are what they asked for.

Nothing matched and nothing you may see are different answers and the page must give the second one. A permission-filtered search genuinely returns zero rows, and rendering that as "no such record" teaches somebody that the order they raised was never saved. The page names the registers that were not searched and who opens them — a person and a role, never "your administrator" — and it never says how many hidden records matched. Naming a closed register is a fact about the account; naming the number of rows inside it is a fact about the data, and a search box that answers "MS-4821 matched 3 records you may not see" is an oracle anybody can query one string at a time.

There is no create action anywhere on this page, in any state. That is empty-state's rule about a filtered register, and it is sharper here: the whole premise of a search is that the record might exist, so a New order button under "nothing matched" is the shortest path to raising the same order twice. The way out of an empty result is a wider query, not a new record.

A facet's own counts are computed with that facet's predicate removed and every other predicate in force. Tick Silvassa with the counts computed naively and Vapi reads 0, so the facet you just used is the one facet you can no longer use. This is a server fact and not something the browser works out — the counts arrive with the results and the page draws them.

A facet that does not apply to every group is not drawn until the type is chosen. A value band over a mixed result silently drops every vendor and every item from the answer, because they have no value to be in a band, and the count under the h1 falls by a hundred for a reason nothing on screen explains. The band appears the moment the type facet narrows to orders or invoices, and it goes again when it widens.

A facet value at zero keeps its place and stops being a control. Removing it makes the list a different shape on every query, so nobody can find the value they set last week, and the value that vanished is indistinguishable from one the register never had. Rendering it as a disabled checkbox is worse again — a dead tab stop that explains nothing. It becomes plain grey text with its 0 beside it, which is the whole explanation, sitting where it always sits.

Loading draws the facets for real and the results as a flat run of grey rows with no headings. The group shape is precisely the thing that is not known yet, so three headings with rows under them is a promise the answer will probably break — and a skeleton that reflows on arrival is worse than a spinner, because a spinner never promised a layout. The facet rail is drawn because it is largely the same rail every query gets; its counts are blank rather than stale, since last query's numbers beside this query's box are wrong in a way nobody can see.

A bare /search shows recent searches and recently opened records, and the recent searches carry no counts. "MS-4821 — 303 results" recorded last Tuesday is a number that has since changed and that nobody can check, and it is read as current. The query and when it was run is all that is true. These are the palette's recents made browsable: the same list, longer, at a URL, with real links in it.

The query language is optional and, where it exists, an unrecognised key is text and never an error. value:10l typed by somebody who read half the help is searched as the literal string, the page says so and names the fields that do exist, and the results still arrive. A search box that returns a parse error for a typo is a search box people stop using; the recognised keys are echoed as removable chips whose only source of truth is the box itself, so removing a chip edits the string and there is no second copy of the query to drift.

Below lg the rail cannot be a rail. The facets become a bottom sheet whose trigger carries the number in force, and the one facet everybody uses — record type — is promoted out of the sheet into a row of pills that scrolls sideways in its own box. The chips never go into the sheet: they are the answer to what is applied, and a phone that hides the filters without saying which are on is a search that looks broken and cannot be diagnosed.

The h1 is the query that produced this page and not what is currently in the box. They diverge the moment somebody starts typing a new search, and that is right: the heading names the answer on screen, and rewriting it as the caret moves would relabel the results under the reader with a query that has not been run. The box is the next query; the h1 is this one.

On a page template the preamble is an HTML comment and carries no template tags at all, which is the one place the two comment forms are not interchangeable. Django wants the extends tag first and tests that against the first non-text node, so a comment tag above extends raises where raw text does not — and an HTML comment is not a Django comment, so a comment tag written inside one as prose opens a real comment block and swallows the template to the next endcomment. Below the extends line the rule inverts and every block of prose is a real comment tag, because a multi-line hash comment is not a comment and renders from its second line on.

The snippet root is a bounded scroller — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box, and the facet sheet is absolute inset-0 against that frame. As a real page it renders inside app-shell's <main>: drop the wrapper's height and border, keep the mx-auto max-w-[1600px] gutter on the band and on the body so the h1 and the results line up, and make the sheet fixed inset-0.

anatomy.description: page-header's <header> inside <main>: white, edge to edge over a border-zinc-200 rule, its content in the same mx-auto max-w-[1600px] gutter the results use. Holds the box, the h1 and the two status lines and nothing else.

input's search markup — bordered wrapper, the icon inside it, type="search", enterkeyhint="search", a clear button that only exists while there is a value and hands focus back when it acts. It carries the query that produced the page, not a placeholder.
The one h1, and it is the query: Results for “MS-4821”. Scoped to one type it becomes Purchase orders matching “MS-4821”. Group headings below it are h2.
A role="status" in the document from first paint, saying how many results in how many registers. Facets, scoping and a new query all rewrite it; it never arrives with its message already in it.
What was searched and what was not — the registers this account may read, named. Present on every state, because the answer means something different depending on it.
An <aside> at lg with its own h2, one fieldset per facet, every value carrying its own count. Below lg it is a sheet behind a trigger that carries the number in force.
One removable chip per facet value in force, with Clear all as a link beside them, in data-table's exact shape. Visible at every width, including when the controls have gone into the sheet.
One white card per record type: an h2 with the type's name, the true count, and where it is truncated the link to the scoped page. Three rows, and the group is the unit that gets ordered.

Designed per record type and carrying the register's own facts. A stretched anchor over the whole row, a status dot in a line box where the record has a state, and a grey clause naming the field that matched when the match is not visible on the row.
The region above the groups when the query is one document number: the record itself, drawn as its identifying band rather than as a row, and not repeated in the group below.
empty-state's shape in the results column — one graphite well, the headline naming the query, what was searched, and the looser query offered with its real count. No create action, in any state.
The recessed band under an empty result naming the registers that were not searched and the person who opens them. It carries no count of what is hidden.
skeleton's row shape with no headings over it, standing in the results column while the query is in flight, aria-busy on the column and aria-hidden on the pulse wrapper.

behaviour: Enter in the box navigates to a new URL carrying the query; it does not filter what is on screen. Every facet, every scope and every page of a scoped result is a parameter on that URL, so Back returns to the previous answer and the current one can be sent to somebody else.

Results are grouped by record type and the groups are ordered by the best match inside them, tiebroken by a fixed register order. Every group states its true count, shows the first three rows, and where there are more the header links to the scoped page.

A group heading is where narrowing starts. Following it scopes the page to that one type: the h1 changes, the facets change to the ones that type has, the register's own sort appears, and a link back to all results sits above the h1.
A query that is exactly one document number promotes that record to its own region above the groups and does not navigate to it. The record does not appear again in the group below.

Facet counts arrive with the results. Ticking a value re-runs the query, rewrites the count line, rebuilds the chips and returns a scoped result to its first page. A value at zero is drawn where it belongs, as text, and cannot be ticked.
A facet that only applies to some record types is drawn only while the type is narrow enough for it to mean something, and disappears again when the type widens.

Nothing matched shows what was searched, offers the loosened query with the count it would return, and offers the two searches this page cannot run itself. It never runs the looser query silently and never offers to create the record.
Where the account cannot read a register, the page says which register and who grants it, on every state, and never how many rows are behind it.

While a query is in flight the box keeps its value, the facets stay drawn with their counts blank, and the results column is a flat run of grey rows with no headings — the group shape is what is being waited for.
A bare /search shows recent searches with when they were run, and recently opened records in the same row shapes the results use. No recent search carries a count.

Below lg the facets are a sheet, the record type is a row of pills scrolling in its own box, and the chips stay on the page. The sheet closes on Escape and on its own button, and focus returns to the trigger.
Nothing on this page scrolls sideways at 390px. The only region allowed to is the record-type pill row, because a second line of pills reads as a different control.
accessibility: One <main>, one <h1>, and the h1 is the query. Group headings are h2, the facet rail's own heading is an h2, and the empty state's headline is an h2 as well — an empty search page still has an outline.

The query box precedes the h1 because it precedes it on screen and the two orders must not disagree. It is a <form role="search"> holding a labelled input, and the label says what is searched rather than repeating the word Search.

The count line is a role="status" rendered with the page, so a facet, a scope or a new query writes into a region that was already there. A live region that arrives with its message in it has not changed and is announced to nobody.

The result list inside a group is a <ul role="list"> — the role is written because the divide and the padding remove the list semantics in Safari — and each row is one <li> with one stretched anchor naming the record.

The stretched anchor is the row's accessible name and it names the record, not the row: PO-2026-0418, never "view". A second link inside the row sits above the stretched one on relative z-10 so it is separately reachable, and the row lights up on has-[a:focus-visible] so the keyboard sees what the pointer sees.
A status dot is aria-hidden and the state is a sr-only word at the front of the meta line, so nothing on this page is carried by colour alone.

The facet rail is an <aside> with an accessible name, and each facet is a <fieldset> with a real <legend>. The count is inside the label rather than beside it, so the checkbox is announced as "Purchase orders, 186" and not as "Purchase orders" with a loose number after it.
A facet value at zero is not a control at all. It is text in the same position, so it is read in place and is not a tab stop that does nothing.
Each chip's remove button names the facet it drops — "Remove the filter Plant: Silvassa", never "Remove" — because six buttons called Remove is what gets read out otherwise.

While the query is in flight the results column carries aria-busy="true", the pulse wrapper carries aria-hidden="true", and one sr-only role="status" outside that wrapper says what is being searched. Three jobs, and collapsing any two loses one.

The facet sheet is a role="dialog" with aria-modal, a focus trap, Escape closing it and focus returning to the trigger, and the trigger carries the number in force in its own text rather than in a title.
The empty state's explanation is text and not an aria-label, and the looser query is offered as a real button whose name contains the query it would run.
